column4: The section explicitly hears غَيْرُ مَمْنُونٍ as an unmeasured, undiminished wage; this ayah says the patient are paid أَجْرَهُم بِغَيْرِ حِسَابٍ, making that reading concrete.
The section explicitly invokes this ayah: faithful righteous work is admitted to the Garden and is not underpaid even by a نَقِيرًا, the tiniest pit in a date stone.
The deathbed challenge calls its addressees غَيْرَ مَدِينِينَ, precisely the section's د ي ن sense of being liable for repayment or recompense.
The resurrected skeptic asks whether death and dust will leave him لَمَدِينُونَ, directly voicing disbelief that a final recompense will be exacted.
The section explicitly links this return to the whole accounting image: creatures are returned to their true Master, الحكم belongs to Him, and He is swiftest in حساب.
The section cites this ayah as the first half of its closing ledger: the assessed human being's return is to God.
Following 88:25's return, this ayah assigns their حساب to God, completing the section's movement from appraisal to final settlement.
Faith and righteous work receive أَجْرٌ غَيْرُ مَمْنُونٍ, the exact reward formula whose measured yet uncurtailed force the section develops.
This ayah repeats the section's exact pairing of faith, righteous works, and أَجْرٌ غَيْرُ مَمْنُونٍ outside surah 95.
The promise أَجْرًا غَيْرَ مَمْنُونٍ supplies another direct Quranic setting for a payment that is neither cut down nor exhausted.
Just scales are set for resurrection, no soul is wronged, and even a mustard seed is brought to account: the section's assay becomes an explicitly eschatological weighing.
God's setting of the ميزان alongside the raised heaven gives the commercial balance a created and moral order.
This ayah forbids transgression in the balance set in 55:7, marking the boundary between sound assay and corrupted measure.
أَقِيمُوا ٱلْوَزْنَ بِٱلْقِسْطِ joins the section's ق و م root to exact, just weighing and expressly forbids making the scale deficient.
The warning to المطففين names the moral opposite of the section's full-weight coin.
The defrauders demand full measure when they receive, exposing a self-serving standard of value.
They diminish what they measure or weigh out to others, the direct reversal of a full-weight payment.
The question whether such traders expect resurrection carries the market scene into the final reckoning.
This ayah identifies the resurrection anticipated in 83:4 as a tremendous day, when crooked measures are answered for.
People stand before the Lord of the worlds, joining the market ledger to the wider ق و م field of standing for judgment.
God will يُوَفِّيهِمُ ٱللَّهُ دِينَهُمُ ٱلْحَقَّ: دِين is their true due and God pays it in full, almost a compact statement of the section's payment reading.
إِذَا تَدَايَنتُم بِدَيْنٍ stages the named د ي ن sense literally: a deferred debt is measured, written, witnessed, and protected from diminution.
A qintar and a single دينار test two trustees; one returns the deposit and one withholds it unless pressed, bringing coin, exact value, and repayment into one moral assay.
Betrayed property must be brought on resurrection, after which every soul is paid in full for what it earned and none is wronged; fraudulent taking and exact settlement share one ayah.
The invitation is expressly to pay Moses أَجْرَ مَا سَقَيْتَ لَنَا, a literal wage for completed work that anchors the section's أجر as work's return.
Mothers who nurse are to be given أُجُورَهُنَّ, a concrete labor payment whose fairness grounds the eschatological wage image.
God creates, causes death, and يردّ some people to the most abject age; the same ر د د movement turns human fitness back toward incapacity.
In an argument for resurrection, some humans are يُرَدُّ إِلَىٰ أَرْذَلِ ٱلْعُمُرِ until knowledge is lost, closely paralleling the section's reversal from fine making to low condition.
Whomever God grants long life He reverses in creation, a nonlexical parallel to the image of a well-formed human losing the condition in which he was first assayed.
خَلَقَكَ فَسَوَّىٰكَ فَعَدَلَكَ depicts the human as created, proportioned, and balanced before the surah confronts denial of recompense.
This ayah completes 82:7 by saying God assembled the human in whatever form He willed, specifying the Maker behind the body's sound proportion.
كَلَّا بَلْ تُكَذِّبُونَ بِٱلدِّينِ is the closest direct echo of surah 95's question about denying دِين after being created and balanced.
The repeated question وَمَا أَدْرَىٰكَ مَا يَوْمُ ٱلدِّينِ magnifies the day on which the section's debt is settled.
The second formulation repeats and intensifies the demand to reckon with يَوْمُ ٱلدِّينِ rather than dismiss it.
On that day no soul controls anything for another and the command belongs to God, defining the final Judge's exclusive authority.
God commands trusts to be returned and judgment between people to be made with justice, directly enacting the section's definition of حكم as a just decision.
وَمَنْ أَحْسَنُ مِنَ ٱللَّهِ حُكْمًا is a rhetorical counterpart to أَحْكَمِ ٱلْحَاكِمِينَ and opposes God's judgment to the judgment of ignorance.
A wrongdoer would offer everything on earth as ransom, but judgment is made بالقسط and no one is wronged, showing that the final account cannot be bought off.
At the final gathering the record and witnesses are brought and judgment is rendered بالحق without injustice, staging the section's just closing of the books.
Following 39:69's judgment, every soul is paid in full for what it did, the exact settlement after valuation.
ٱلْوَزْنُ يَوْمَئِذٍ ٱلْحَقُّ makes the resurrection's weighing true, and heavy scales identify those whose value endures.
Light scales expose people who have made themselves lose, an explicit counterpart to the coin that fails assay and falls among the worthless.
Heavy scales at judgment mark the successful, repeating the section's full-weight standard in eschatological form.
Light scales mean self-loss and lasting punishment, the moral analogue of failing the money changer's test.
The one whose مَوَازِينُ are heavy passes the judgment's assay.
A pleasing life is the outcome assigned to the heavy scales of 101:6, showing what that weight is worth.
Light مَوَازِينُ make the principal reversal vivid: apparent human holdings carry insufficient weight.
The light scales lead downward to an abyss, turning loss of weight into the lowest destination.
The command to fulfill measure and weight بالقسط, followed by the rule that no soul bears beyond capacity, binds exact commerce to exact moral charge.
Shuayb commands full measure and weight and forbids diminishing people's goods, a literal market version of undiminished payment.
Shuayb forbids reducing measure and weight while warning of an encompassing day, connecting crooked valuation with judgment.
Full measure, just weight, and the ban on depriving people of their things define the honest assay against which the section's coin is tested.
بَقِيَّتُ ٱللَّهِ خَيْرٌ contrasts the gain God leaves with profit made by false measure, a direct valuation of what truly remains.
The ayah commands full measure and weighing with the straight balance, then calls that better in final outcome.
Fulfilling the measure and refusing to make others losers states the payment ethic in literal commercial terms.
The straight balance is the section's full-standard coin tested by an honest scale.
The prohibition on diminishing people's goods identifies social corruption as a falsified valuation.
The measuring commands culminate in fear of the One who خَلَقَكُمْ, joining just commercial measure to the Creator who measured human beings.
Book and ميزان are sent so people may uphold justice, making the scale an instrument of divine social judgment rather than a merely commercial tool.
A day of return to God ends with every soul paid in full for what it earned and no injustice, a concise version of the section's entire account.
On the undoubted gathering day every soul is paid in full for what it earned and none is wronged.
Death precedes the day when people are paid أُجُورَكُمْ in full; the ayah then devalues worldly life as deceptive merchandise.
God does not wrong even an atom's weight, multiplies a good deed, and grants a great wage, combining minute assay and generous payment.
A good deed receives tenfold while an evil one receives only its like, and neither side is wronged; final payment is exact yet gracious.
Each person is fully repaid for deeds, and God's complete knowledge secures the accuracy of the settlement.
Every soul comes pleading for itself, is fully paid what it did, and is not wronged: the worker meets the account personally.
The judgment permits no injustice and recompenses people only for what they did, stating exact equivalence between work and return.
Each soul is recompensed for what it earned, with no injustice and a swift حساب, directly joining wages to the final ledger.
Creation in truth has the purpose that every soul be recompensed for what it earned without injustice, linking خَلْق and measured return.
People receive ranks according to their works so that God may pay their deeds in full without wrong, uniting labor, valuation, and payment.
A human has only what he strove for, establishing the work side of the section's wage equation.
The striving named in 53:39 will be seen, so no work escapes appraisal.
The seen striving is then repaid with the fullest repayment, completing work, assessment, and wage.
Even an atom's weight of good is seen, a minute assay below which no earned value disappears.
Even an atom's weight of evil is seen, making the same scale exact on the debit side.
These petitioners have a نَصِيبٌ مِّمَّا كَسَبُوا and God is swift in account, directly joining an allotted share to what was earned.
Those who exchange God's covenant for a small price receive no خَلَاقَ in the Hereafter, uniting false pricing with the section's measured-share sense of the word.
Men and women each have a نَصِيبٌ from what they earned, a clear Quranic form of the allotted share attached to work.
The two cultivators receive unlike returns: the Hereafter's harvest is increased, while the worldly cultivator gets some of it but no نَصِيبٍ in the Hereafter.
What people possess runs out while what is with God remains, and the patient are paid their wage by the best of their works; permanence and payment meet explicitly.
Believing workers of righteousness receive a good life and a wage based on the best they did, matching the section's work-for-wage account.
Wealth and children are temporary adornment, while enduring good deeds are better with the Lord in reward and hope, an explicit divine appraisal.
Enduring righteous deeds are declared better with the Lord in reward and return, measuring lasting work against transient holdings.
The addressees prefer the nearer life, identifying the mistaken valuation that the section's assay exposes.
The Hereafter is better and more lasting, supplying the corrected value judgment after 87:16.
Those who spend without following their gift by مَنّ or injury retain their wage; the other Quranic sense of م ن ن shows how a payment can be spoiled by being held over its recipient.
Charity is invalidated by مَنّ and injury like soil stripped from a smooth rock, a vivid case of apparent value failing when assayed.
A human reads generous provision as God's declaration that he is honored, exposing a faulty human method of appraisal.
When provision is measured tightly, the same human concludes he is humiliated; the pair shows that market quantity is not God's final valuation.
No action and no atom's weight escapes the clear record, giving the final appraisal exhaustive precision.
A mustard seed hidden in rock, heaven, or earth is brought forth by God, so even concealed moral weight enters the account.
Not an atom's weight, smaller, or greater escapes God; all is in a clear record used to answer the denial of resurrection.
Yusuf is sold for a paltry price in counted dirhams because the sellers assign him little value, a human undervaluation of a finely made person.
Those whose works collapse through denial receive no وَزْنًا on resurrection; نُقِيمُ also brings the section's ق و م field into a judgment where failed deeds have no assay value.
Hypocrites are assigned to the lowest depth of the Fire, turning the section's س ف ل baseness into an exact eschatological rank.
God makes the disbelievers' word السُّفْلَىٰ and His word highest, a direct high-low judgment of worth.
أَتَسْتَبْدِلُونَ ٱلَّذِى هُوَ أَدْنَىٰ بِٱلَّذِى هُوَ خَيْرٌ rebukes exchanging the lower for the better, the section's valuation error stated as a failed trade.
Even an earthful of gold cannot be accepted as ransom from one who dies rejecting faith, setting a boundary on coin's power at the final account.
All the earth and as much again cannot ransom disbelief from punishment, so worldly holdings cannot discharge this debt.
Those who refuse their Lord would offer the earth twice over as ransom, yet theirs is the evil account; no proposed payment can revise the appraisal.
Wrongdoers would ransom themselves with everything on earth doubled, but the judgment discloses a liability wealth could not price.
Hoarded gold and silver that are not spent become grounds for painful punishment, reversing stored monetary value.
The treasured metal is heated and used to brand its owners, turning the coin-like asset itself into evidence in the account.
Those who want only worldly display are paid their works in full here and suffer no shortfall here, a deliberately limited settlement.
The same works prove void in the Hereafter and yield only Fire, showing that a payment received in one market may carry no final value.
Disbelieving works become ashes scattered by a violent wind, leaving their owners unable to retain any of what they earned.
The question identifies the greatest losers by their works, inviting appraisal of labor that its workers mistakenly count as valuable.
Their effort is lost in worldly life while they think they are doing fine work, the self-deception of a failed assay.
After 18:105 removes all weight from their deeds, this ayah names their recompense as Hell for denial and mockery.
Disbelieving deeds are a mirage that looks like water until nothing is found; instead the person finds God, who pays his account in full.
Works that appeared substantial are made scattered dust, a direct image of value rejected at divine inspection.
The question asks whether wealth and children are being advanced as proof of good value, exposing a mistaken reading of worldly provision.
The answer says they do not perceive the truth, refusing wealth and offspring as a reliable divine appraisal.
Wealth and children do not bring people near; faith and righteous work receive multiplied recompense, correcting the market's status scale.
The person who gathers and repeatedly counts wealth treats enumeration as security and value.
He imagines his wealth makes him permanent, confusing counted property with enduring worth.
The hoarder is instead cast into the Crusher, the final rejection of his self-assessed value.
Whatever good is spent is repaid in full and the spender is not wronged, a charitable instance of exact settlement.
Those who believe and do righteous works are paid their wages in full, and the denial of love for wrongdoers guards the judgment's justice.
Faithful righteous workers are paid their wages fully and receive additional bounty, showing that exact payment need not exclude grace.
Whatever is spent in God's way is repaid in full without injustice, another concrete outlay-and-return account.
Faithful righteous action need fear neither injustice nor diminution, making non-reduction the result of the final assay.
Belief removes fear of both unfair loss and oppressive excess, setting boundaries on the account in both directions.
The Garden is called a recompense and the recipients' striving is thanked, linking recognized labor to its payment.
جَزَاءً وِفَاقًا describes a recompense fitted to the deed, the debit side of equivalent settlement.
The Lord's جَزَاءً عَطَاءً حِسَابًا presents the reward as an ample, reckoned gift, balancing measure and generosity.
God says He does not let the work of any worker be lost, making the worker's identity and labor answerable to an unfailing payer.
God does not waste the wage of anyone who does good work, a direct statement that sound workmanship retains its value.
The promised dwellings for faithful good workers end with نِعْمَ أَجْرُ ٱلْعَامِلِينَ, explicitly joining أجر and عاملين.
The inheritors of the Garden call it نِعْمَ أَجْرُ ٱلْعَامِلِينَ, recognizing the final allotment as the workers' excellent wage.
God pays the reciters and spenders their wages in full and adds from His bounty, a settlement greater than strict equivalence.
God removes the worst of faithful workers' deeds and pays their wage according to the best, identifying the standard used in valuation.
A good loan to God is multiplied many times and all are returned to Him, translating lending into eschatological return.
The covenant asks for a good loan to God and promises expiation and gardens, a debt idiom whose return exceeds the advance.
The one who lends God a good loan receives it multiplied and an honorable wage, placing loan and wage in one account.
Charitable men and women who lend the good loan receive multiplication and a noble wage, specifying who is credited.
A good loan is multiplied and forgiven, so divine repayment includes both credited increase and canceled liability.
Good sent ahead is found with God as better and greater in wage, while the good loan figures as the advance entered in that account.
Moses notes that a wage could have been taken for repairing the wall, another literal job-price that clarifies أجر.
The proposal to hire Moses values strength and trustworthiness as the qualities of a good paid worker.
Pharaoh's magicians ask whether there will be an أجر if they prevail, showing wage as a promised return for performance, though from a corrupt payer.
The magicians again seek a wage for victory, a literal payment bargain that contrasts with divine recompense.
Yusuf describes himself as one who gives full measure, making honest provision the opposite of curtailed payment.
The brothers find their merchandise returned and anticipate obtaining measure again, bringing ر د د into a concrete exchange-and-provision setting.
In hardship the brothers ask Yusuf to fulfill the measure and treat the excess as charity, distinguishing an exact commercial due from a gift.
Created stores are sent down only in a known measure, a cosmic version of provision being allotted rather than random.
God creates everything and determines it with exact determination, grounding measured value in the Creator's act rather than the market alone.
Everything is created بِقَدَرٍ, directly supporting the section's link between خَلْق and measure.
God has made a measure for everything, setting a universal boundary beside the reward that is not curtailed.
God apportions livelihoods among people and raises some in degrees so they serve one another, a worldly instance of measured shares.
Unlimited worldly provision would provoke transgression, so God sends it by the measure He wills; measured livelihood is a boundary distinct from uncurtailed reward.
God creates and proportions, a concise parallel to the human being made fit before valuation.
God determines and guides, extending proportion into an assigned course and end.
God forms humans and makes their forms good, then provides good things and identifies Himself as their Lord, joining good formation to provision and return.
God forms humans and makes their forms good, and the ayah ends with the destination to Him, linking fine formation with eventual return.
The staged human creation culminates in another creation and praise of the best of creators, a Quranic appraisal of formed humanity.
Creation moves from weakness to strength and back to weakness and grayness, another arc in which human condition loses its initial force.
مَٰلِكِ يَوْمِ ٱلدِّينِ names God as sovereign of the day when recompense is due, the title under which the section's account closes.
Abraham hopes for forgiveness on يَوْمِ ٱلدِّينِ, showing that the day of payment also admits mercy.
At resurrection the deniers recognize هَٰذَا يَوْمُ ٱلدِّينِ, the day whose liability they had questioned in 37:53.
وَإِنَّ ٱلدِّينَ لَوَٰقِعٌ states that the promised recompense will certainly fall due.
The mockers ask when يَوْمُ ٱلدِّينِ will be, another stance of disbelief toward the due account.
The punishment is identified as the guests' reception on يَوْمِ ٱلدِّينِ, the hostile payout for their course.
Those who affirm يَوْمِ ٱلدِّينِ embody the believing stance opposite the denial challenged in surah 95.
The condemned confess that they used to deny يَوْمِ ٱلدِّينِ, showing denial entered as a charge in the final reckoning.
The wicked enter the Fire on يَوْمِ ٱلدِّينِ, giving the term's recompense sense a concrete outcome.
The transgressing deniers are those who deny يَوْمِ ٱلدِّينِ, carrying the crooked-scale passage into explicit denial of settlement.
أَرَءَيْتَ ٱلَّذِى يُكَذِّبُ بِٱلدِّينِ echoes surah 95's challenge, then tests that denial by its treatment of vulnerable people.
Shuayb asks God to judge between the two groups in truth and calls Him the best of judges, locating fair judgment within the same prophet's market dispute.
The command is to wait until God judges, followed by وَهُوَ خَيْرُ ٱلْحَٰكِمِينَ, a close verbal counterpart to surah 95's final question.
Noah addresses God as أَحْكَمُ ٱلْحَٰكِمِينَ while asking about a painful family case, placing supreme judgment above a human claim.
Jacob is entrusted to decide until God judges, and God is called the best of judges, distinguishing patient human waiting from final decision.
If judgment is undertaken it must be بالقسط, and God loves those who act equitably, explaining what the supreme Judge's حكم looks like in human practice.
إِنِ ٱلْحُكْمُ إِلَّا لِلَّهِ reserves judgment to God, whose true decision separates the parties.
The plea رَبِّ ٱحْكُم بِٱلْحَقِّ asks the Lord to judge in truth, the proper stance before the section's final Judge.
God gathers the parties and judges between them in truth, uniting final assembly with the decisive valuation.
David is commanded to judge people in truth and not follow desire, a human office measured against the just divine حكم.
Each person's record is fastened to him and will be brought out as an open book, giving the account an individual ledger.
The command to read one's own book makes the person sufficient as reckoner against himself.
The record omits neither small nor great, deeds are found present, and the Lord wrongs no one, an exhaustive audit.
A record speaks truth and no one is wronged, while no soul is charged beyond capacity; assessment and evidence match.
Each community kneels and is summoned to its record, staging the judicial opening of communal ledgers.
God's record speaks truth because deeds were copied, explaining the evidence behind the payment in 45:22.
Everything the wrongdoers did is in the records, so no work vanishes before assessment.
Every small and great thing is inscribed, defining the ledger's precision.
One petitioner asks only for this world and has no خَلَاقٍ in the Hereafter, showing an allotted share lost through narrow valuation.
Worldly goods are temporary enjoyment and adornment, while what is with God is better and lasting, a direct comparison of appraised value.
A person promised the good promise and meeting it is contrasted with one briefly provisioned then brought for judgment.
People dazzled by Qarun call his display a mighty fortune, voicing a worldly market appraisal.
Those given knowledge answer that God's reward is better for faithful good workers and is received by the patient, correcting 28:79's valuation.
The flower of worldly life is only a test, while the Lord's provision is better and more lasting.
Worldly possessions are temporary enjoyment, while what is with God is better and more enduring for believers.
Worldly life swells like admired growth then becomes debris, while the Hereafter holds punishment or forgiveness; the ayah exposes temporary apparent value.
People break away for trade and diversion, but what is with God is better than both and He is the best provider, a market choice corrected from the pulpit.
Worldly enjoyment is called little, the Hereafter better for the God-fearing, and no one is wronged even by a thread on a date stone.
Satisfaction with the nearer life is rebuked because its enjoyment is only little beside the Hereafter.
Expanded or restricted provision does not alter that worldly life is only a small enjoyment beside the Hereafter.
The believing speaker calls this worldly life temporary enjoyment and the Hereafter the lasting home.
Even imagined gold adornment is only worldly enjoyment, whereas the Hereafter with the Lord belongs to the God-fearing.
People do not reach full righteousness until they spend from what they love, making surrendered value part of the assay.
Believers must not select defective goods for giving when they themselves would accept them only with eyes closed; payment must carry value the payer recognizes.
Recitation, prayer, and spending are called a trade that will never perish, preparing for the full wage in 35:30.
God purchases believers' lives and wealth for the Garden and calls it the greatest triumph, a divine exchange that assigns their highest price.
Buying error for guidance yields a trade with no profit, a moral misvaluation expressed in market terms.
Those who purchase worldly life with the Hereafter receive unabated punishment, a disastrous exchange between passing and lasting value.
Buying error for guidance and punishment for forgiveness treats final liabilities as a ruinous exchange.
The covenant must not be exchanged for a small price because what is with God is better, a direct refusal of undervaluation.
A debtor in hardship receives deferment, and remission is better; the literal debt relation introduces mercy into exact accounting.
Creditors retain only their principal, neither wronging nor being wronged, defining a just boundary for repayment.
The companions send a silver coin to purchase food and seek what is purest; it is a literal coin scene, though it does not itself stage final appraisal.
After 56:86 challenges those claiming they owe no recompense, this ayah demands that they return the departing soul if truthful; تَرْجِعُونَهَا makes ر د د the test of that claim.
God recompenses workers by the best they did, adds from His bounty, and provides without account, joining appraised work to payment beyond a curtailed measure.
A believer who works righteousness enters the Garden and is provided there without account, a close parallel to the section's unmeasured wage.
The blessed remain in the Garden through an عَطَاءً غَيْرَ مَجْذُوذٍ, an uncut gift that states without م م ن wording what the section hears in غَيْرُ مَمْنُونٍ.
The declaration that God's provision has no exhaustion directly parallels a reward whose amount is neither cut down nor used up.
Those who purchase magic know that its buyer has no خَلَاقٍ in the Hereafter, and the ayah condemns the price for which they sold themselves; measured share and ruinous valuation meet explicitly.
People consume their خَلَاق as earlier peoples consumed theirs and end with void works, showing an allotted worldly share spent without retaining final value.
God is قَائِمًا بِٱلْقِسْطِ and declares His unique divinity with the witnesses, joining the ق و م field to the maintenance of exact justice.
The command to be قَوَّامِينَ بِٱلْقِسْطِ requires testimony against self or kin and refuses to let wealth or poverty distort the appraisal.
Believers must stand firmly as just witnesses and not let hatred cause an inequitable judgment, bringing ق و م into the practice of the section's just measure.
إِنِ ٱلْحُكْمُ إِلَّا لِلَّهِ reserves judgment to God and then calls exclusive worship ٱلدِّينُ ٱلْقَيِّمُ, bringing حكم, د ي ن, and ق و م together in their rule-and-uprightness senses.

The command to set one's face to the dīn invokes the fitrah upon which God خَلَقَ people and calls it ٱلدِّينُ ٱلْقَيِّمُ, joining creation, proportionate fit, and the semantic range of دِين and ق و م.
The upright book is قَيِّمًا and immediately promises faithful righteous workers a good wage, placing moral straightness and recompense in one ayah.
The recipient of the book in the right hand receives an easy حساب, making the manner of final settlement explicit.
The joyful recipient of the record explains that he expected to meet his حساب, joining present valuation to prior accountability.
The recipient of the other record laments that he did not know what his حساب would be, the stance that leaves the account disastrously unpaid.
The mockers demand that their قِطَّنَا, their allotted portion, be hastened before the Day of Account, turning a measured share into sarcasm about final payment.
Every soul is held for what it earned, and no ransom or equivalent payment is accepted apart from God, combining liability, earnings, and the impossibility of buying off the account.
Each soul earns only against itself, bears no other's burden, and returns to the Lord for disclosure, joining personal earnings to final return.
The human begins as a drop, then is created and proportioned; this repeats the sound formation that precedes the question of resurrection and recompense.
God creates the human from a drop and measures or proportions him, a direct creation-side counterpart to the section's assayed human being.
Those given their record in the right hand read it and are not wronged even by a tiny thread, combining the ledger with minute exactness.
No soul can settle for another on the judgment day and no equivalent ransom is accepted, setting a firm boundary on debt transfer and payment.
The ayah calls the price for which they sold themselves evil: rejection born of envy turns the self into badly valued merchandise.
Those who conceal revelation purchase only a small price and consume fire, so apparent market gain is reassessed as punishment.
People throw the scripture behind them and purchase a small price, which the ayah judges an evil acquisition.
Believers from the People of the Book do not exchange God's signs for a small price and therefore retain their wage with their Lord.
The command not to exchange God's signs for a small price makes faithful judgment the alternative to corrupt valuation.
Selling God's signs for a small price leads people to block His way, exposing the moral cost hidden by the quoted price.
Those who manufacture scripture for a small price receive woe both for what their hands wrote and for what they earned, turning fraudulent production into a debit.
Apostasy through death makes works void in both worlds, a direct case of accumulated labor losing all final assay value.
Denial and murderous opposition leave deeds void in this world and the Hereafter, so no final value remains.
Whoever rejects faith has his work voided and becomes one of the losers in the Hereafter, the result of failed moral assay.
Even the named prophets' works would be void if they associated partners, stating the boundary under which work retains value.
Denying God's signs and the meeting of the Hereafter voids works, and the question says they receive only the recompense of what they did.
The self-claimed service of shrine-tending cannot survive open disbelief; its workers' deeds are declared void.
Those sparing with support and abusive after fear passes have their works nullified by God, so outward participation proves debased.
Association would nullify even the addressee's work and place him among the losers, an explicit warning that the coin of labor can fail completely.
Ruin is pronounced upon the disbelievers and their deeds are led astray, beginning a direct account of lost work.
Because they hate what God sent down, He makes their works void, identifying why the labor in 47:8 loses value.
Following what angers God and hating His pleasure results in works being nullified, another stated cause of failed assay.
Those who disbelieve, bar the way, and oppose the messenger cannot harm God, but their own works are nullified.
Believers are expressly warned not to nullify their works, presenting retained value as something obedience must guard.
Believers must spend before a day on which no trade, friendship, or intercession operates, marking the end of ordinary market remedies.
Spending must occur before the day with neither bargaining nor friendship, so present wealth cannot be offered after the account opens.
The day when neither wealth nor children benefit rejects the two common human measures of worth.
No ransom is accepted from hypocrites or disbelievers; the final liability cannot be discharged with a substitute payment.
The plotters against Abraham are made ٱلْأَسْفَلِينَ, turning their intended mastery into divinely assigned lowness.
The condemned ask to place their human and jinn misleaders underfoot among ٱلْأَسْفَلِينَ, exposing the end-value they now assign their former guides.
The command not to give with a view to obtaining more uses the other م ن ن field to forbid treating generosity as an investment seeking enlarged return.
Receiving the record in the right hand supplies the documentary scene that makes the easy account of 84:8 intelligible.
Receiving the record from behind the back marks the rejected side of the ledger before the call for destruction.
The successful person is handed his record in the right hand and invites others to read it, the visible presentation preceding his statement about حساب in 69:20.
The failed person receives the record in the left hand and wishes it had never been given, setting up his ignorance of the account in 69:26.
Worldly life is made attractive to disbelievers, while God provides the God-fearing without account on resurrection, correcting apparent present value.
God gives provision without account to whom He wills, a non-wage formulation of quantity unbounded by ordinary reckoning.
Mary receives provision from God without account, making unmeasured giving concrete within a sanctuary scene.
Property is something God made قِيَامًا for people, preserving the ق و م sense of that by which life stands rather than merely its assessed price.
People who certify their own purity are corrected: God appraises whom He wills and wrongs no one even by a tiny thread.
God honors the children of Adam, provides them good things, and favors them over much creation, a divine valuation of the human being.
God makes good everything He created and begins human creation from clay, another Quranic statement of sound created workmanship.
After 75:38's created and proportioned human, this ayah asks whether that Maker can raise the dead, carrying formation into final accountability.
Forgiveness and enduring gardens are called the excellent wage of workers, another explicit worker-to-wage formulation.
The faithful rejoice that God does not waste the believers' wage, stating preservation of earned value.
Those who hold to the Book and establish prayer are assured that God does not waste the wage of reformers.
Recorded thirst, fatigue, and effort are justified by the rule that God does not waste the wage of good-doers.
Every expenditure and journey is written so that God may recompense the best of the workers' deeds, joining ledger entry and wage.
Patience is commanded because God does not waste the wage of good-doers, a preservation counterpart to the uncurtailed payment.
Yusuf's earthly establishment illustrates that God does not waste the wage of good-doers, though the payment here begins before the final account.
Joseph links reverence and patience to the principle that God does not waste the wage of good-doers.
The father offers marriage in return for eight years of Moses' service and leaves two more voluntary, specifying a negotiated term of labor after 28:26's hiring proposal.
The command not to exchange God's signs for a small price identifies revelation as something market valuation must not cheapen.
One person sells himself seeking God's pleasure, a positive self-exchange whose value is fixed by its divine object.
Those who purchase disbelief with faith cannot harm God and receive painful punishment, another exchange that reveals its true price only at judgment.
Those given a share of scripture purchase error and wish others to lose the way, spending received value on loss.
The call to fight addresses those who sell the worldly life for the Hereafter and promises a great wage whether slain or victorious.
Witnesses must not exchange their oath for a price even when kin could benefit, preserving truthful valuation in an estate account.
Purchasing distracting speech to mislead others turns expenditure into a humiliating liability.
The Lord decides the disputes of the Children of Israel by His حكم, specifying the knowledgeable and powerful Judge behind the decision.
The answer to rejected exclusive worship is that الحكم belongs to God, the Exalted and Great, reserving final decision to Him.
Whatever people dispute has its حكم with God, and the speaker turns back to Him, joining decision and return.
